title: Houthi attacks on southern Saudi Arabia wound 73, ignite oil facilities on September 8
dek: The Houthis launched coordinated drone and ballistic missile strikes on Saudi cities and oil infrastructure on September 8, wounding 73 people according to Saudi officials. The attacks mark the most serious escalation since a 2022 UN-brokered truce and threaten global energy supplies and Red Sea shipping routes.
author: The GoCheckMyNews Desk
key_fact: According to Major General Turki al-Malki, the Saudi-led coalition spokesperson, the Houthi attacks on September 8 wounded 73 people, including women and children, and ignited fires at oil facilities and utilities in the Saudi cities of Abha, Jazan, Najran and Khamis Mushait.
bottom_line: The escalation hinges on whether Saudi Arabia and the Houthis can return to sustained negotiations, which Prince Faisal suggested remained possible despite the military response. A key indicator will be whether regional counteroffensives near al-Makha and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait advance territorial control or stall, as the Houthis have linked ground gains directly to their capacity to sustain pressure on Red Sea shipping.
body: The Houthis launched a coordinated wave of drone and ballistic missile attacks across southern Saudi Arabia on Tuesday, September 8, wounding 73 people and igniting fires at oil facilities and utilities, according to Major General Turki al-Malki, spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition. The strikes hit civilian and economic facilities in the Saudi cities of Abha, Jazan, Najran and Khamis Mushait, and targeted Jazan City for Primary and Downstream Industries, a major industrial and logistics hub on Saudi Arabia's southwestern Red Sea coast, as well as Aramco facilities in Najran and Abha and King Khalid Air Base in Khamis Mushait.

The renewed hostilities represent the most serious escalation since a UN-brokered truce halted large-scale fighting in 2022, after eight years of full-blown conflict. The attacks threaten global energy supplies and maritime traffic through one of the world's most critical shipping corridors.

Houthi military spokesman Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree claimed responsibility for the strikes, saying the group fired dozens of ballistic missiles and drones at oil and economic facilities, as well as an air base. Saree blamed Saudi Arabia for the escalation, warning that "every aggression against our country and people will be met with a firm response." Nasruddin Amer, deputy head of the Houthi media office, stated on social media: "The Saudi enemy has to understand that the time for committing crimes and massacres against the Yemeni people without response, deterrence or paying a price has ended."

The Houthis linked their attacks to a Saudi airstrike that, per Houthi claims, hit a prison in Yemen's northern province of Jawf, killing at least seven people, including a child, and wounding seven others in the city of Hazem. According to NPR's reporting, a coalition airstrike struck the runway of Sanaa airport in late August, preventing the landing of a flight from Tehran to Yemen's capital Sanaa, challenging a decade-long air and naval blockade by the Saudi-led coalition.

The Jazan refinery in Saudi Arabia's southern region has a capacity of 400,000 barrels per day, making it one of the kingdom's largest, per NPR reporting. In 2024, approximately 4.1 million barrels of crude oil and petroleum products passed through the Bab al-Mandeb Strait daily on average, representing about 5 percent of global total, according to Al Jazeera. Between March and mid-July 2026, Saudi seaborne crude exports through Bab al-Mandeb were eight times higher than during the same period in 2025, per Al Jazeera. The Houthis declared a blockade against Saudi shipping in July.

Al-Malki called the attacks a "serious escalation" and a "flagrant violation of the kingdom's sovereignty, and a direct threat to the security and safety of its citizens and residents." The Saudi-led coalition vowed retaliation, saying it "will take all necessary operational measures to deter the terrorist Houthi militia with utmost resolve." Saudi Arabia's foreign minister Prince Faisal Bin Farhan al Saud stated the kingdom "strongly condemns" the Houthi attacks and said "The Houthis choose to prioritise their narrow interests over the interests of Yemen and resort to violence."

Prince Faisal also said, "The road to diplomacy is not closed. Saudi Arabia will always support diplomatic solutions, but the kingdom will never hesitate to defend itself and its interests. We will use every tool to do our job and our duties." According to Ahmed Nagi, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, the Houthis' movement toward the western coast connects their ground campaign to maritime strategy: "The Houthis have already linked their military campaign to the Red Sea and the shipping routes around Bab al-Mandeb. So gaining more control over the western coast could give them greater depth and allow them to sustain pressure on maritime traffic in the Red Sea."

The latest escalation has displaced approximately 18,500 people in Taiz and Hodeida in southwestern Yemen, per NPR reporting. Abdusattor Esoev, IOM Yemen's Chief of Mission, said: "Families are arriving with nothing: no shelter, no food, no way to know if it's safe to go back" and "Many of these are people who have already been displaced once, twice, even four times before." Yemen's civil war began in 2014 when the Houthis seized Sanaa and much of northern Yemen and forced the government into exile. A Saudi-led coalition intervened in 2015 to try to restore the government to power. The conflict has killed at least 150,000 people according to UN estimates, per NPR.
